interactions.label: In Tetralogy of Fallot, squatting during a cyanotic spell relieves symptoms beca

params.question: In Tetralogy of Fallot, squatting during a cyanotic spell relieves symptoms because it:

answers.text: Increases venous return to the right atrium, improving cardiac output

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Increased venous return alone does not correct the shunt. Squatting compresses the femoral arteries, raising systemic vascular resistance — this makes the pulmonary route relatively more favourable for blood flow.

answers.text: Raises systemic vascular resistance, reducing the right-to-left shunt across the VSD

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Compressing the femoral arteries raises systemic vascular resistance above right ventricular outflow resistance, diverting more blood through the pulmonary circuit and improving oxygenation.

answers.text: Directly lowers pulmonary vascular resistance, increasing lung blood flow

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Squatting does not directly lower pulmonary vascular resistance. The benefit comes from raising systemic vascular resistance, making the pulmonary circuit the path of lesser resistance across the VSD.

answers.text: Causes reflex bradycardia that lengthens diastolic filling time

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bradycardia is not the mechanism of relief. Squatting raises systemic vascular resistance by compressing the femoral arteries, reducing the right-to-left shunt that causes cyanosis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the haemodynamics of TOF. The fixed pulmonary stenosis creates a right-to-left shunt whose magnitude depends on the ratio of systemic to pulmonary vascular resistance.
Well done. Understanding the SVR–PVR balance across the VSD is key to explaining both tet spells and why squatting provides relief.

interactions.label: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, heart failure occurs primarily because:

params.question: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, heart failure occurs primarily because:

answers.text: The ventricular walls become thin and flabby, reducing systolic contractility

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Thin, flabby walls describe dilated cardiomyopathy, which causes systolic failure. In HCM, sarcomere gene mutations drive thickening of the septum, not thinning.

answers.text: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy impairs ventricular filling during diastole

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Sarcomere mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3) drive asymmetric septal hypertrophy that stiffens the left ventricle and may obstruct the outflow tract, causing diastolic failure. Myofibre disarray on microscopy is the hallmark.

answers.text: Amyloid deposition uniformly stiffens the myocardium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Amyloid infiltration characterises restrictive cardiomyopathy, not HCM. In HCM, the hypertrophy is asymmetric and driven by sarcomere protein mutations, with disorganised myofibre architecture.

answers.text: Viral myocarditis destroys cardiomyocytes, reducing functional muscle mass

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Viral myocyte destruction (e.g. by Coxsackievirus B) characterises myocarditis, which may progress to dilated cardiomyopathy. HCM is a genetic sarcomere disease, not an infectious process.

overallFeedback.feedback: Revisit the three cardiomyopathy types. HCM = diastolic failure from asymmetric septal hypertrophy; DCM = systolic failure from ventricular dilatation; RCM = stiff ventricle from infiltrative disease.
Exactly right. Distinguishing diastolic failure (HCM) from systolic failure (DCM) is fundamental to cardiomyopathy classification.

interactions.label: In acute rheumatic fever, Group A beta-haemolytic streptococci directly invade t

params.question: In acute rheumatic fever, Group A beta-haemolytic streptococci directly invade the heart and cause tissue destruction.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Unlike infective endocarditis where organisms colonise the valve, rheumatic fever is driven by molecular mimicry. Antibodies raised against streptococcal M-protein cross-react with cardiac proteins, causing immune-mediated damage without any direct bacterial invasion of the heart.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this is false. No bacteria enter the heart in rheumatic fever. The damage is entirely immune-mediated: cross-reactive antibodies against streptococcal M-protein target cardiac myosin and valve glycoproteins (Type II hypersensitivity), amplified by T-cell responses (Type IV).

interactions.label: In intravenous drug users with tricuspid valve endocarditis, the expected emboli

params.question: In intravenous drug users with tricuspid valve endocarditis, the expected embolic complication is:

answers.text: Cerebral infarction causing stroke

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Stroke results from left-sided endocarditis, where vegetations embolise into the systemic arterial circulation. Right-sided vegetations on the tricuspid valve drain into the pulmonary arteries, not the cerebral vessels.

answers.text: Multiple septic pulmonary infiltrates

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Tricuspid valve vegetations fragment and travel through the right heart into the pulmonary arteries, producing multiple septic emboli visible as pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-ray.

answers.text: Painful nodules on the fingertips (Osler nodes)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Osler nodes are immune-complex-mediated lesions seen in left-sided subacute endocarditis. In right-sided disease, emboli travel to the lungs, not to the peripheral vasculature.

answers.text: Splenic and renal cortical infarcts

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Splenic and renal infarcts result from systemic emboli in left-sided endocarditis. Right-sided endocarditis directs emboli exclusively through the pulmonary circulation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: the tricuspid valve sits on the venous side. Its vegetations embolise through the right ventricle to the pulmonary arteries, causing lung infiltrates — not systemic infarcts.
Exactly. Understanding the embolic pathway — right-sided to lungs, left-sided to systemic organs — is essential for diagnosing and managing infective endocarditis.

interactions.label: A patient with pericardial effusion develops cardiac tamponade. Which factor mos

params.question: A patient with pericardial effusion develops cardiac tamponade. Which factor most critically determines whether tamponade occurs?

answers.text: The absolute volume of pericardial fluid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Volume alone is not decisive. A slow 2-litre effusion can be tolerated because the pericardium stretches gradually. A rapid 200 mL collection can cause tamponade because the pericardium has no time to accommodate.

answers.text: The rate at which fluid accumulates in the pericardial space

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The pericardium can stretch to accommodate large volumes if fluid accumulates slowly. Rapid accumulation — even as little as 200 mL — raises intrapericardial pressure abruptly, compressing the right heart and producing Beck's triad.

answers.text: The viscosity and protein content of the fluid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fluid composition plays no significant role in tamponade physiology. The critical variable is how quickly intrapericardial pressure rises relative to pericardial compliance — a function of accumulation rate, not fluid properties.

answers.text: The patient's underlying left ventricular ejection fraction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tamponade is a mechanical problem — external compression of the heart by rising intrapericardial pressure. It can occur even with normal systolic function; the key determinant is the rate of fluid accumulation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Focus on the pericardial compliance curve. Slow accumulation allows gradual stretching; rapid accumulation exceeds compliance, raising intrapericardial pressure and compressing the right heart — producing Beck's triad.
Well done. This rate-versus-volume principle explains why post-surgical bleeding causes tamponade with small volumes, while chronic effusions can grow very large without haemodynamic compromise.

interactions.label: Cardiac myxoma characteristically causes posture-dependent syncope because:

params.question: Cardiac myxoma characteristically causes posture-dependent syncope because:

answers.text: The tumour secretes vasoactive peptides that lower blood pressure on standing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Although myxomas can produce systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss), posture-dependent syncope is mechanical. The pedunculated mass swings into the mitral valve orifice when the patient changes position.

answers.text: The pedunculated mass prolapses through the mitral valve, intermittently obstructing blood flow

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Myxoma arises near the fossa ovalis in the left atrium on a stalk. With posture changes, gravity shifts the gelatinous mass into the mitral orifice, intermittently obstructing ventricular filling and causing syncope.

answers.text: It compresses the cardiac conduction system, producing intermittent heart block

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Conduction system compression could cause arrhythmias but would not vary specifically with posture. The syncope in myxoma is due to mechanical obstruction of the mitral valve by the pedunculated tumour mass.

answers.text: Tumour fragments embolise to the cerebral arteries, causing transient ischaemic attacks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Embolisation from a friable myxoma does cause stroke, but this produces fixed neurological deficits, not posture-dependent syncope. The syncope results from intermittent mechanical obstruction of the mitral valve.

overallFeedback.feedback: Myxoma sits on a stalk near the fossa ovalis. Its pedunculated anatomy explains why posture changes shift the mass into the mitral orifice, intermittently blocking blood flow and causing syncope.
Exactly right. The combination of left atrial origin, pedunculated morphology, and mitral valve obstruction makes posture-dependent syncope a classic myxoma presentation.
